title: Historical currency values in 2025 US dollars

methodology.summary: Each value answers: 'how many 2025 US dollars buy the same basket of consumer goods that one base unit of this currency bought in that year?' (a CPI / 'real price' comparison).
steps: Express the currency in a contemporary anchor money: pounds sterling for years up to 1910 (via metal content, legal parity, or exchange rate), US dollars for years from 1915 (via exchange rate).
Carry the anchor amount to 2025 with a consumer price index: UK — Bank of England millennium dataset (1209-2016) spliced to ONS CPI D7BT (2017-2025); US — Minneapolis Fed CPI (1800-2025).
Convert 2025 pounds to dollars at the 2025 annual average ($1.3192/£, Federal Reserve G.5A).

Before 1717 gold coins are valued through English silver coinage using an estimated gold:silver ratio; from 1717 through the British gold standard (£1 = 7.3224 g fine gold) and market gold:silver ratios.
Antiquity and Edo-period Japan have no price index: values are commodity-price equivalences (wheat, barley, rice), with the wage-based equivalent given as the upper end of the range.
caveats: CPI comparisons understate how 'big' a sum felt: before c.1900 a day's wage bought far fewer goods, so a wage- or income-share comparison can be 3-10× higher than the CPI value. Use the 'high' end of the range for social context.
The sterling-route and dollar-route for the same moment can differ by tens of percent because US and UK prices moved differently (purchasing-power-parity gaps).
Exchange rates in wartime, under exchange controls, or for inconvertible currencies are official rates and may not reflect what the money could actually buy.
'low' and 'high' are judgement-based bands (high ±10%, medium ×/÷1.35, low ×/÷2, very low ×/÷3 or explicit goods-vs-wage bounds), not statistical confidence intervals.

provenance.computed: Calculated directly from downloaded datasets (BoE, ONS, Minneapolis Fed, Fed G.5A) plus a metal content or parity.
provenance.compiled: Uses an exchange rate, parity, or estimate entered by hand from the cited reference; verify against the source before relying on it.

methodology.interpolation: Between data points, interpolate linearly in log(usd2025). Do not extrapolate beyond a currency's first or last point.
methodology.fictional: Currencies with 'fictional': true come from novels, films and games ('work' names the source). Their 'series' is empty when no real-world value can be justified, or holds a single undated estimate (stored at the year of the cited work) derived from in-world prices and wages. 'sources' at the currency level cite the exchange rates between denominations.
methodology.denominations: Each denomination's 'value' is in base units of its currency. When 'periods' is present, use the period containing the year (inclusive bounds). Years are astronomical-ish integers; negative = BCE.

currencies.name: Pound sterling
currencies.notes: Values are UK consumer-price equivalents (what the money would buy in goods), converted to dollars at the 2025 exchange rate. Pre-1500 index values rest on few commodity prices; for wages or social status the 'feel' of a sum can be several times larger.

denominations.name: Pound (sovereign/quid)
denominations.notes: Before 1971: £1 = 20 shillings = 240 pence. 'l.' (libra) was often used for pounds.

denominations.name: Mark (money of account)
denominations.notes: 13s 4d; an accounting unit, not a coin.

denominations.name: Noble
denominations.notes: Gold coin of 6s 8d.

denominations.name: Angel
denominations.notes: Gold coin; 6s 8d at issue, later raised to 7s 6d, 8s, 10s and 11s.

denominations.name: Sovereign (Tudor)
denominations.notes: Large gold coin: 20s, then 22s 6d, then 30s (the 'fine sovereign').

denominations.name: Guinea
denominations.notes: Gold coin 1663-1814. Floated in value (peaking ~30s in 1694-96) until fixed at 21s in 1717; thereafter 21s and used as an accounting unit (professional fees, horses, art) long after the coin ceased.

denominations.name: Sovereign
denominations.notes: Gold £1 coin from 1817 (7.32 g fine gold).

denominations.name: Crown
denominations.notes: 5 shillings.

denominations.name: Half-crown
denominations.notes: 2s 6d.

denominations.name: Florin
denominations.notes: 2 shillings; introduced 1849 as a step toward decimalisation; continued as the 10p coin.

denominations.name: Shilling
denominations.notes: 12 pence. Coin from 1504; before that a unit of account. After 1971 = 5p.

denominations.name: Groat
denominations.notes: 4 pence.

denominations.name: Penny (old)
denominations.notes: 'd' for denarius. 240 to the pound.

denominations.name: Farthing
denominations.notes: Quarter penny.

currencies.name: Spanish dollar (peso, real de a ocho)
currencies.region: Spain, Spanish America; global trade coin
currencies.notes: Valued by its silver content against English silver coinage (to 1716) or the gold standard with market gold:silver ratios (from 1717). The Mexican peso (1821-) continued the same coin and is effectively this currency.

denominations.name: Maravedí
denominations.notes: 34 maravedís to the real (money of account).

denominations.name: Escudo (gold)
denominations.notes: Gold; roughly 2 dollars (16 reales) in the 18th century.

denominations.name: Pistole (2 escudos)
denominations.notes: Two-escudo gold piece, ≈ 16-17s sterling; called a 'pistole' in English and French.

denominations.name: Doubloon (8 escudos / onza)
denominations.notes: 'Doubloon' in English usually means the 8-escudo onza (≈ £3 6s sterling); it could also mean the 2-escudo piece.

currencies.name: Livre tournois
currencies.notes: Values follow the silver content of the livre. Low confidence before c.1550: medieval France saw frequent royal debasements and recoinages not captured at 5-year resolution. John Law's paper system (1719-20) makes 1720 especially uncertain.

denominations.name: Livre (tournois)
denominations.notes: Money of account: 1 livre = 20 sous = 240 deniers. 'Franc' was a common synonym.

denominations.name: Liard
denominations.notes: 3 deniers.

denominations.name: Gros tournois
denominations.notes: Silver coin worth 1 sou at issue.

denominations.name: Écu d'or
denominations.notes: Gold écu; its value in livres rose as the livre was debased (fixed at 60 sous in 1577).

denominations.name: Écu (silver, 'écu blanc')
denominations.notes: Large silver coin; 6 livres from 1726. The 'petit écu' was half that.

denominations.name: Louis d'or
denominations.notes: Gold coin; 24 livres from 1726 (until the 1785 recoinage kept it at 24 with less gold).

denominations.name: Pistole (accounting)
denominations.notes: 10 livres; also the name for Spanish 2-escudo pieces.
